claim: Many mammalian cancer cell lines depend on glutamine as a major tri-carboxylic acid (TCA) cycle anaplerotic substrate to support proliferation.
source: Many mammalian cancer cell lines depend on glutamine as a major tri-carboxylic acid (TCA) cycle anaplerotic substrate to support proliferation.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer cell metabolism supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Some cell lines that depend on glutamine anaplerosis in culture rely less on glutamine catabolism to proliferate in vivo.
source: However, some cell lines that depend on glutamine anaplerosis in culture rely less on glutamine catabolism to proliferate in vivo.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Davidson et al., 2016) and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells cultured in adult bovine serum exhibit decreased glutamine catabolism compared to cells cultured in standard tissue culture conditions.
source: We find that cells cultured in adult bovine serum, which better reflects nutrients available to cells in vivo, exhibit decreased glutamine catabolism and reduced reliance on glutamine anaplerosis compared to cells cultured in standard tissue culture conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing isotope labeling patterns in different culture conditions.

claim: Adult bovine serum better reflects nutrients available to cells in vivo than standard tissue culture media.
source: We find that cells cultured in adult bovine serum, which better reflects nutrients available to cells in vivo, exhibit decreased glutamine catabolism and reduced reliance on glutamine anaplerosis compared to cells cultured in standard tissue culture conditions.
evidence: This is based on the authors' reasoning about nutrient composition and comparison to in vivo conditions.

claim: Cystine levels account for the differential dependence on glutamine in different environmental contexts.
source: We find that levels of a single nutrient, cystine, accounts for the differential dependence on glutamine in these different environmental contexts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that cystine supplementation alone can recapitulate the phenotype.

claim: Cystine levels dictate glutamine dependence via the cystine/glutamate antiporter xCT/SLC7A11.
source: Further, we show that cystine levels dictate glutamine dependence via the cystine/glutamate antiporter xCT/SLC7A11.
evidence: This is supported by knockdown and overexpression experiments showing the requirement for xCT/SLC7A11.

claim: xCT/SLC7A11 expression, in conjunction with environmental cystine, is necessary and sufficient to increase glutamine catabolism.
source: Thus, xCT/SLC7A11 expression, in conjunction with environmental cystine, is necessary and sufficient to increase glutamine catabolism, defining important determinants of glutamine anaplerosis and glutaminase dependence in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by genetic manipulation experiments and metabolic tracing studies.

claim: Altered metabolism is a hallmark of cancer.
source: Altered metabolism is a hallmark of cancer (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011) and reflects the increased energetic and biosynthetic demands of proliferating cancer cells (DeBerardinis and Chandel, 2016; Vander Heiden and DeBerardinis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Increased glucose uptake and glycolysis in tumors is one of the earliest noted biochemical differences between cancerous and normal tissues.
source: Indeed, one of the earliest noted biochemical differences between cancerous and normal tissues is increased glucose uptake and glycolysis in tumors (Cori and Cori, 1925; Warburg et al., 1927).
evidence: This is supported by historical citations to foundational work.

claim: Many cancer cells consume substantial amounts of glutamine in culture, far in excess of other amino acids.
source: Beyond increased glucose metabolism in tumors, another long standing observation is that many cancer cells consume substantial amounts of glutamine in culture, far in excess of other amino acids (Eagle, 1955; Jain et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Many cancer cell lines depend on extracellular glutamine for proliferation in vitro.
source: Consistent with this, many cancer cell lines depend on extracellular glutamine for proliferation in vitro, even though glutamine is nominally non-essential and can be synthesized from other nutrients.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Glutamine can be synthesized from other nutrients.
source: Consistent with this, many cancer cell lines depend on extracellular glutamine for proliferation in vitro, even though glutamine is nominally non-essential and can be synthesized from other nutrients.
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Glutamine is a proteinogenic amino acid.
source: It is a proteinogenic amino acid, can act as a nitrogen donor for the synthesis of amino acids as well as nucleotides, and glutamine can contribute carbon to the TCA cycle to replace cycle intermediates that are removed for the production of biomass, a process termed anaplerosis (Altman et al., 2016; Daye and Wellen, 2012; DeBerardinis and Cheng, 2010; Hensley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by established biochemical knowledge and citations.

claim: Glutamine can act as a nitrogen donor for the synthesis of amino acids and nucleotides.
source: It is a proteinogenic amino acid, can act as a nitrogen donor for the synthesis of amino acids as well as nucleotides, and glutamine can contribute carbon to the TCA cycle to replace cycle intermediates that are removed for the production of biomass, a process termed anaplerosis (Altman et al., 2016; Daye and Wellen, 2012; DeBerardinis and Cheng, 2010; Hensley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by established biochemical knowledge and citations.

claim: Glutamine can contribute carbon to the TCA cycle to replace cycle intermediates removed for biomass production (anaplerosis).
source: It is a proteinogenic amino acid, can act as a nitrogen donor for the synthesis of amino acids as well as nucleotides, and glutamine can contribute carbon to the TCA cycle to replace cycle intermediates that are removed for the production of biomass, a process termed anaplerosis (Altman et al., 2016; Daye and Wellen, 2012; DeBerardinis and Cheng, 2010; Hensley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by established biochemical knowledge and citations.

claim: Most glutamine nitrogen is excreted as ammonia and alanine in proliferating cancer cells in vitro.
source: Analysis of the fate of glutamine nitrogen in proliferating cancer cells in vitro suggests that most glutamine nitrogen is excreted as ammonia and alanine, suggesting that the high rate of glutamine consumption is not due to nitrogen demand (DeBerardinis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The high rate of glutamine consumption is not due to nitrogen demand.
source: Analysis of the fate of glutamine nitrogen in proliferating cancer cells in vitro suggests that most glutamine nitrogen is excreted as ammonia and alanine, suggesting that the high rate of glutamine consumption is not due to nitrogen demand (DeBerardinis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited data about nitrogen excretion.

claim: Glutamine metabolism is important for TCA cycle anaplerosis in multiple contexts.
source: Instead, glutamine metabolism is important for TCA cycle anaplerosis in multiple contexts (Altman et al., 2016; DeBerardinis et al., 2007; Yuneva et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The majority of aspartate, glutamate and TCA cycle metabolites are glutamine-derived across cancer cell lines.
source: Across cancer cell lines, the majority of aspartate, glutamate and TCA cycle metabolites are glutamine-derived (Altman et al., 2016; Wise and Thompson, 2010), with production of amino acids being a major fate of anaplerotic glutamine carbon (Hosios et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Production of amino acids is a major fate of anaplerotic glutamine carbon.
source: Across cancer cell lines, the majority of aspartate, glutamate and TCA cycle metabolites are glutamine-derived (Altman et al., 2016; Wise and Thompson, 2010), with production of amino acids being a major fate of anaplerotic glutamine carbon (Hosios et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Proliferation of many cell types following glutamine starvation is rescued by providing α-ketoglutarate.
source: In line with these results, proliferation of many cell types following glutamine starvation is rescued by providing an alternative source of the TCA cycle intermediates α-ketoglutarate (αKG) (van den Heuvel et al., 2012; Wise et al., 2008; Wise et al., 2011) or oxaloacetate (Patel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Proliferation of many cell types following glutamine starvation is rescued by providing oxaloacetate.
source: In line with these results, proliferation of many cell types following glutamine starvation is rescued by providing an alternative source of the TCA cycle intermediates α-ketoglutarate (αKG) (van den Heuvel et al., 2012; Wise et al., 2008; Wise et al., 2011) or oxaloacetate (Patel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Anaplerosis contributes to the large cellular consumption of glutamine in culture.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that anaplerosis contributes to the large cellular consumption of glutamine in culture, and to dependence on this amino acid for cell proliferation and survival.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies.

claim: ASCT2/SLC1A5 and LAT1/SLC7A5 have higher expression in certain tumors.
source: Relevant to cancer, the neutral amino acid transporters ASCT2/SLC1A5 and LAT1/SLC7A5 are known to have higher expression in certain tumors, and can mediate glutamine uptake in cell lines derived from these tumors (Bhutia et al., 2015; Pochini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ASCT2/SLC1A5 and LAT1/SLC7A5 can mediate glutamine uptake in cell lines derived from tumors.
source: Relevant to cancer, the neutral amino acid transporters ASCT2/SLC1A5 and LAT1/SLC7A5 are known to have higher expression in certain tumors, and can mediate glutamine uptake in cell lines derived from these tumors (Bhutia et al., 2015; Pochini et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Glutaminase activity can be the primary driver of glutamate production from glutamine in proliferating cells.
source: In proliferating cells, glutaminase activity can be the primary driver of glutamate production from glutamine, as amide nitrogen incorporation into mass is low compared to release of glutamine nitrogen as ammonia (Brand, 1985; Brand et al., 1986; Hosios et al., 2016; Wise et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Genetic or pharmacological loss of GLS1 activity depletes TCA metabolites and slows proliferation of a variety of cancer cell lines in culture.
source: Genetic or pharmacological loss of GLS1 activity depletes TCA metabolites and slows proliferation of a variety of cancer cell lines in culture (Cheng et al., 2011; Gameiro et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2009; Gross et al., 2014; Le et al., 2012; Seltzer et al., 2010; Son et al., 2013; Timmerman et al., 2013; van den Heuvel et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2010; Yuneva et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The glutaminase inhibitor CB-839 is being evaluated in clinical trials to treat cancer.
source: This has led to interest in targeting glutaminase activity therapeutically, and the glutaminase inhibitor CB-839 is being evaluated in clinical trials to treat cancer (Gross et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents factual information about clinical trials.

claim: Rapidly proliferating cells preferentially use transamination reactions for αKG production.
source: Rapidly proliferating cells have been shown to preferentially use transamination reactions for αKG production, consistent with their increased need for nitrogen for biosynthetic demand (Coloff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Glutamine catabolic pathways are controlled by oncogene expression and upregulated in many cancer cell lines.
source: Finally, consistent with these observations of increased glutamine catabolism and dependence in rapidly proliferating cultured cells, glutamine catabolic pathways are controlled by oncogene expression and upregulated in many cancer cell lines (Altman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Human NSCLC and mouse KRAS-driven NSCLC tumors rely more on glucose than on glutamine for TCA cycle anaplerosis.
source: Tracing of glucose and glutamine fate in tumors derived from human non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and mouse KRAS-driven NSCLC found that these tumors rely more on glucose than on glutamine for TCA cycle anaplerosis (Davidson et al., 2016; Hensley et al., 2016; Sellers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: NSCLC tumors are resistant to glutaminase inhibition in vivo.
source: This correlated with resistance of these tumors to glutaminase inhibition in vivo; but surprisingly, cell lines derived from these tumors with decreased glutamine catabolism showed dramatically increased glutamine anaplerosis and sensitivity to glutaminase inhibition when cultured in vitro (Davidson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Cell lines derived from NSCLC tumors show increased glutamine anaplerosis and sensitivity to glutaminase inhibition when cultured in vitro.
source: This correlated with resistance of these tumors to glutaminase inhibition in vivo; but surprisingly, cell lines derived from these tumors with decreased glutamine catabolism showed dramatically increased glutamine anaplerosis and sensitivity to glutaminase inhibition when cultured in vitro (Davidson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Environmental differences between tumors in vivo and tissue culture dictate the use of glutamine for anaplerosis.
source: These results suggest that, even for cells capable of glutamine catabolism, environmental differences between tumors in vivo and tissue culture dictates the use of glutamine for anaplerosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies.

claim: A549 cells cultured in adult bovine serum exhibit ~35% of glutamate derived from glutamine.
source: In fact, only ~35% of glutamate was estimated to be derived from glutamine when cells were cultured in adult bovine serum.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from isotope tracing studies.

claim: Glutamine labeling reached isotopic steady state after 8 hr of culture in adult bovine serum.
source: We verified that glutamine labeling reached isotopic steady state after 8 hr of culture in adult bovine serum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that these labeling differences were not explained by differences in labeling kinetics.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: The decrease in glutamine-derived label in A549 cells cultured in adult bovine serum is not specific to bovine serum or serum products.
source: Importantly, the decrease in glutamine-derived label observed in A549 cells cultured in adult bovine serum was not specific to bovine serum or to serum products, as the contribution of glutamine carbon to glutamate and TCA cycle intermediates was similarly reduced in adult bovine heparinized plasma and adult human serum (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Reduced TCA cycle labeling from glutamine when cells are cultured in adult bovine serum is not limited to A549 cells.
source: Reduced TCA cycle labeling from glutamine when cells are cultured in adult bovine serum is not limited to A549 cells. [U-13C5]glutamine labeling of TCA cycle intermediates was higher in cell lines derived from cancers arising in diverse tissues when cultured in RPMI compared to culture in adult bovine serum (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: A549 cells cultured in RPMI are sensitive to CB-839.
source: Consistent with these findings, we find that A549 cells cultured in RPMI are also sensitive to CB-839, but the same cells become resistant to CB-839 when cultured in adult bovine serum (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A549 cells become resistant to CB-839 when cultured in adult bovine serum.
source: Consistent with these findings, we find that A549 cells cultured in RPMI are also sensitive to CB-839, but the same cells become resistant to CB-839 when cultured in adult bovine serum (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A549 cells cultured in bovine serum exhibit decreased glutamine metabolism and are resistant to glutaminase inhibitors, adopting a metabolic phenotype similar to lung tumors in vivo.
source: Thus, A549 cells cultured in bovine serum exhibit decreased glutamine metabolism and are resistant to glutaminase inhibitors, adopting a metabolic phenotype with regards to glutamine metabolism that is more similar to lung tumors in vivo than to lung cancer cells cultured in standard tissue culture media.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Differences in the small molecule fraction between RPMI and adult bovine serum account for differences in glutamine use for TCA cycle anaplerosis.
source: Taken together, these experiments suggest that differences in the small molecule fraction of standard tissue culture media and adult bovine serum largely explain the differences in glutamine anaplerosis and glutaminase inhibitor sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on dialysis experiments showing that small molecules are responsible for the phenotype.

claim: RPMI and DMEM contain excess glucose, amino acids and micronutrients compared to blood.
source: RPMI and DMEM both contain excess glucose, amino acids and micronutrients compared to blood (Mayers and Vander Heiden, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation and comparison of nutrient concentrations.

claim: Re-formulation of DMEM to have more physiological concentrations of nutrients alters central carbon metabolism and glutamine dependence.
source: In fact, re-formulation of DMEM to have more physiological concentrations of glucose, amino acids and other nutrients were previously reported to alter central carbon metabolism and glutamine dependence (Schug et al., 2015; Tardito et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Addition of RPMI nutrients to adult bovine serum results in increased glutamine contribution to the TCA cycle in A549 cells.
source: Addition of RPMI nutrients (glucose, amino acids, vitamins and micronutrients) to adult bovine serum resulted in increased glutamine contribution to the TCA cycle in A549 cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of nutrients to adult bovine serum to levels found in RPMI or DMEM causes increased A549 sensitivity to CB-839.
source: Addition of nutrients to adult bovine serum to levels found in either RPMI or DMEM also caused increased A549 sensitivity to CB-839 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Addition of amino acids alone at RPMI levels to adult bovine serum increases glutamine contribution to the TCA cycle to the same extent as addition of all RPMI nutrients.
source: Addition of amino acids alone at RPMI levels to adult bovine serum increased glutamine contribution to the TCA cycle to the same extent as addition of the whole pool of all RPMI nutrients (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Addition of amino acids alone at RPMI levels induces CB-839 sensitivity.
source: Addition of amino acids alone at RPMI levels also induced CB-839 sensitivity (Figure 3B), as did addition of amino acids to DMEM levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Only cystine addition triggers sensitivity to CB-839 among serine, glycine, threonine and cystine.
source: Serine, glycine, threonine or cystine were individually increased to DMEM levels in adult bovine serum containing DMEM levels of other amino acids. Only cystine addition triggered sensitivity to CB-839 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Addition of cystine alone to adult bovine serum is sufficient to sensitize cells to CB-839.
source: Addition of cystine alone to adult bovine serum is sufficient to sensitize cells to CB-839 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Addition of cystine at RPMI levels to adult bovine serum causes an increase in glutamine labeling of TCA cycle intermediates comparable to cells cultured in adult bovine serum with all RPMI nutrients.
source: Similarly, addition of cystine at RPMI levels to adult bovine serum causes an increase in glutamine labeling of TCA cycle intermediates that is comparable to the labeling pattern observed in cells cultured in adult bovine serum containing levels of all nutrients found in RPMI (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cystine levels in adult plasma are 4-10 fold lower than in DMEM or RPMI.
source: Cystine levels in adult plasma (~20–50 µM) are 4–10 fold lower than in DMEM or RPMI (~200 µM) (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on measured concentrations shown in Table 1.

claim: High levels of cystine found in standard tissue culture formulations cause enhanced glutamine anaplerosis and dependence.
source: These experiments demonstrate that high levels of cystine found in standard tissue culture formulations cause enhanced glutamine anaplerosis and dependence.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Both TCA cycle metabolites and reduced glutathione levels decrease in A549 cells cultured in RPMI and exposed to CB-839.
source: Both TCA cycle metabolites and reduced glutathione (GSH) levels were decreased in A549 cells cultured in RPMI and exposed to CB-839 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that high cystine-driven use of glutaminase is required for both TCA cycle anaplerosis and maintenance of glutathione.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: CB-839 treatment causes increased levels of DCFDA staining, indicating ROS levels increase following glutaminase inhibition.
source: CB-839 treatment also caused increased levels of DCFDA staining, indicating ROS levels increase following glutaminase inhibition, which was reversible by co-treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Increased ROS following CB-839 treatment is reversible by co-treatment with N-acetylcysteine.
source: CB-839 treatment also caused increased levels of DCFDA staining, indicating ROS levels increase following glutaminase inhibition, which was reversible by co-treatment with N-acetylcysteine (NAC) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Treatment of cells with dimethyl α-ketoglutarate or glutathione monoethyl ester can rescue the proliferation of CB-839 treated A549 cells.
source: Treatment of cells with dimethyl α-ketoglutarate or glutathione monoethyl ester was able to rescue the proliferation of CB-839 treated A549 cells, albeit to differing extents (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Dimethyl α-ketoglutarate treatment rescues both TCA metabolite pools and GSH levels in CB-839 treated cells.
source: However, assessment of TCA cycle metabolite and GSH levels in cells rescued with dimethyl α-ketoglutarate, showed that this rescued both TCA metabolite pools and GSH levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: A549 cells express γ-glutamyl transferase and are able to degrade GSH to replenish glutamate pools.
source: These data are consistent with previous reports showing A549 cells express γ-glutamyl transferase and are able to degrade GSH to replenish glutamate pools (Kang et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: BSO treatment has no effect on A549 proliferation despite GSH depletion to undetectable levels.
source: However, as described previously (Kang et al., 1991), we found that BSO treatment had no effect on A549 proliferation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D) despite GSH depletion to undetectable levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures and citation.

claim: NAC treatment does not rescue cell proliferation following CB-839 treatment.
source: NAC treatment, while able to decrease DCFDA detectable ROS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), did not rescue cell proliferation following CB-839 treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Glutathione depletion and subsequent increase in ROS alone is not sufficient to explain decreased proliferation following glutaminase inhibition in high cystine conditions.
source: Thus, while we have not identified precisely which glutamate dependent metabolic processes are limiting for proliferation upon glutaminase inhibition in high cystine conditions, these data argue that glutathione depletion and the subsequent increase in ROS alone is not sufficient to explain decreased proliferation of these cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The xc– transporter system is composed of xCT (encoded by SLC7A11) and 4F2hc/CD98 (encoded by SLC3A2).
source: This transporter system is composed of the transporter xCT (encoded by SLC7A11) and the chaperone 4F2hc/CD98 (encoded by SLC3A2), and together they mediate the exchange of glutamate for cystine across the plasma membrane (Lewerenz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and established biochemical knowledge.

claim: The xc– transporter system mediates the exchange of glutamate for cystine across the plasma membrane.
source: This transporter system is composed of the transporter xCT (encoded by SLC7A11) and the chaperone 4F2hc/CD98 (encoded by SLC3A2), and together they mediate the exchange of glutamate for cystine across the plasma membrane (Lewerenz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Higher extracellular cystine increases both glutamine and cystine uptake rates as well as glutamate release rate in A549 cells.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that cystine potentiates glutamine anaplerosis by triggering enhanced glutamate secretion via xCT and increased glutamine catabolism, we observed that higher extracellular cystine increased both the glutamine and cystine uptake rates as well as the glutamate release rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) in A549 cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Knockdown of SLC7A11 reduces the glutamine uptake and glutamate release rate of cells cultured in RPMI.
source: We first confirmed that knockdown of SLC7A11 with two hairpins reduced the glutamine uptake and glutamate release rate of cells cultured in RPMI, but did not have a detectable effect on glutamine uptake and glutamate release when cells were cultured in RPMI containing low cystine (10 µM) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Knockdown of SLC7A11 has no consistent effect on steady state intracellular levels of glutamate or glutathione in RPMI or RPMI with low cystine.
source: Knockdown of SLC7A11 had no consistent effect on steady state intracellular levels of glutamate or the glutamate derived metabolite glutathione in either RPMI or RPMI with low cystine (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Knockdown of SLC7A11 substantially decreases the ability of cystine to potentiate glutamine anaplerosis.
source: We found that knockdown of SLC7A11 substantially decreased the ability of cystine to potentiate glutamine anaplerosis, and that this effect was blunted by expression of the shRNA-resistant SLC7A11 cDNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Knockdown of SLC7A11 abrogates CB-839 sensitivity of A549 cells in adult bovine serum with RPMI levels of cystine.
source: Additionally, knockdown of SLC7A11 with multiple hairpins (Figure 4D) abrogated CB-839 sensitivity of A549 cells in adult bovine serum with RPMI levels of cystine (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: xCT/SLC7A11 is necessary for cystine induced glutamine anaplerosis and dependence in A549 cells.
source: Thus, xCT/SLC7A11 is necessary for cystine induced glutamine anaplerosis and dependence in A549 cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the knockdown experiments.

claim: There is a strong correlation between cystine-induced glutamine anaplerosis and xCT/SLC7A11 mRNA expression across cancer cell lines.
source: We found a strong correlation between cystine-induced glutamine anaplerosis and xCT/SLC7A11 mRNA expression reported by the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) (Barretina et al., 2012), suggesting that cystine levels and xCT/SLC7A11 expression contribute to the prominent use of glutamine as a anaplerotic TCA cycle substrate in many cancer cells in culture (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and correlation analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CB-839 sensitive breast cancer cell lines tend to have higher xCT/SLC7A11 expression than resistant lines.
source: Sensitive lines tend to have higher xCT/SLC7A11 expression than resistant lines, suggesting that xCT/SLC7A11 expression may contribute to a requirement for glutaminase in cultured cell lines.
evidence: This is based on comparison of expression data and reported IC50 values.

claim: xCT/SLC7A11 expression increases the incorporation of glutamine carbon into TCA cycle intermediates in the presence of RPMI levels of cystine in MCF7, MDA-MB-468, and AU565 cell lines.
source: xCT/SLC7A11 expression increased the incorporation of glutamine carbon into TCA cycle intermediates in the presence of RPMI levels of cystine in all three cell lines (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: xCT/SLC7A11 expression potentiates CB-839 sensitivity when cells are cultured in RPMI, but not RPMI with 10 µM cystine.
source: xCT/SLC7A11 expression also potentiated CB-839 sensitivity when these cells are cultured in RPMI, but not RPMI with 10 µM cystine (Figure 4J and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: xCT/SLC7A11 is necessary and sufficient for increased glutamine anaplerosis and glutaminase addiction in the presence of high levels of extracellular cystine.
source: These results demonstrate that xCT/SLC7A11 is necessary and sufficient for increased glutamine anaplerosis and glutaminase addiction in the presence of high levels of extracellular cystine.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the genetic manipulation experiments.

claim: An oral dose of 2.4 g/kg cystine can raise plasma cystine levels in mice from ~15 µM to ~70 µM for at least 4 hr.
source: We found that an oral dose of 2.4 g/kg cystine could raise plasma cystine levels in mice from ~15 µM to ~70 µM for at least 4 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Labeling of glutamine, glutamate and αKG from [U-13C5]glutamine in tumors is higher in cystine treated mice.
source: Consistent with increased glutamine catabolism in cystine treated tumors, labeling of glutamine, glutamate and αKG from [U-13C5]glutamine in tumors was higher in cystine treated mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Increasing cystine levels in tumors can cause increased glutamine consumption and glutamate release.
source: These results suggest that increasing cystine levels in tumors can cause increased glutamine consumption and glutamate release, a phenomenon we have shown using in vitro models leads to enhanced glutamine anaplerosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vivo experimental data and in vitro findings.

claim: Low cystine levels in vivo limit tumor glutamine catabolism and anaplerosis.
source: These results are consistent with a model where low cystine levels in vivo limit tumor glutamine catabolism and anaplerosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: High levels of extracellular cystine and the cellular capacity to secrete glutamate in exchange for cystine cooperate to increase glutamine anaplerosis.
source: Thus, high levels of extracellular cystine and the cellular capacity to secrete glutamate in exchange for cystine cooperate to increase glutamine anaplerosis in these cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: GLS1 activity is strongly inhibited by glutamate.
source: The enzymology of glutaminase suggests one potential explanation. GLS1 activity is strongly inhibited by glutamate (Cassago et al., 2012; Curthoys and Watford, 1995) suggesting that the drop in intracellular glutamate driven by high cystine could raise glutaminase activity and increase glutamine contribution to the TCA cycle relative to other pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work on enzyme kinetics.

claim: The drop in intracellular glutamate driven by high cystine could raise glutaminase activity and increase glutamine contribution to the TCA cycle.
source: The enzymology of glutaminase suggests one potential explanation. GLS1 activity is strongly inhibited by glutamate (Cassago et al., 2012; Curthoys and Watford, 1995) suggesting that the drop in intracellular glutamate driven by high cystine could raise glutaminase activity and increase glutamine contribution to the TCA cycle relative to other pathways.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on enzyme kinetics and experimental observations.

claim: xCT/SLC7A11 expression correlates with the ability of cystine to increase glutamine anaplerosis in cell lines from different tumor types and oncogenotypes.
source: xCT/SLC7A11 expression correlates with the ability of cystine to increase glutamine anaplerosis in a panel of cell lines derived from tumors of different oncogenotype and tissue of origin (Figure 4F). This argues that xCT/SLC7A11 expression may be necessary for environmental cystine to enhance glutamine anaplerosis regardless of tumor type, and is not a phenomenon limited to NSCLC and A549 cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data across multiple cell lines shown in Figure 4F.

claim: xCT/SLC7A11 promotes glutamate secretion in human breast cancer cell lines.
source: Indeed, examination of panels of human breast cancer cell lines have found that xCT/SLC7A11 promotes glutamate secretion, providing further evidence that xCT/SLC7A11 can promote glutamine catabolism in cell types beyond NSCLC (Briggs et al., 2016; Timmerman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Glutaminase dependence in culture for many cancer cells will be strongly influenced by both environmental cystine and xCT/SLC7A11 expression.
source: Collectively, these experiments suggest that glutaminase dependence in culture for many cancer cells derived from various tumor types will be strongly influenced by both environmental cystine and xCT/SLC7A11 expression.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings across multiple cell lines.

claim: Assessing xCT/SLC7A11 expression may help identify patients likely to benefit from glutaminase inhibitors.
source: First, assessing xCT/SLC7A11 expression may help identify patients likely to benefit from these drugs.
evidence: This is a therapeutic implication based on the experimental findings.

claim: Not every cancer cell line requires glutamine for proliferation in vitro.
source: While many cancer cells are considered to be glutamine addicted, not every cancer cell line requires glutamine for proliferation in vitro (Cetinbas et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2011; Gross et al., 2014; Timmerman et al., 2013; van den Heuvel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Glutamine dependence has been linked to MYC, RAS, IDH oncogenes and hormone receptor status in breast cancers.
source: Glutamine dependence has been linked to various oncogenes including MYC (Gao et al., 2009; Wise et al., 2008), RAS (Son et al., 2013), IDH (Matre et al., 2014; Seltzer et al., 2010) and hormone receptor status in breast cancers (Gross et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The genetic and biochemical basis for glutamine dependence remains poorly understood.
source: However, the genetic and biochemical basis for glutamine dependence remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: xCT/SLC7A11 expression is governed by the antioxidant response transcription factor NRF2.
source: xCT/SLC7A11 expression is known to be governed by the antioxidant response transcription factor NRF2 (Sasaki et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: xCT/SLC7A11 expression triggered by NRF2-activating drugs can sensitize tumors to glutaminase inhibitors.
source: xCT/SLC7A11 expression triggered by NRF2-activating drugs can sensitize tumors to glutaminase inhibitors (Sayin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Raising tumor cystine levels may increase glutamine anaplerosis in tumors.
source: We found that raising tissue cystine levels may increase glutamine anaplerosis in tumors.
evidence: This is based on the in vivo experimental data.

claim: Co-administration of cystine with glutaminase inhibitors may enhance response to glutaminase inhibitors.
source: Therefore, co-administration of cystine with glutaminase inhibitors may enhance response to glutaminase inhibitors.
evidence: This is a therapeutic speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Oral cystine administration can be effective to raise plasma cystine levels in humans.
source: Oral cystine administration can be effective to raise plasma cystine levels in humans (Morin et al., 1971), arguing that this strategy could be applicable to treating patients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Eagle's medium and RPMI were formulated to identify the minimal set of nutrients required for mammalian cancer cells and leukocytes to rapidly proliferate.
source: Eagle's medium and RPMI were formulated to identify the minimal set of nutrients required for mammalian cancer cells and leukocytes to rapidly proliferate (Eagle, 1955; Moore et al., 1967), not to match physiological levels of nutrients available in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original formulation papers.

claim: Standard tissue culture media lack certain nutrients available to tumors in vivo and contain other nutrients in excess.
source: Thus, these media lack certain nutrients available to tumors in vivo and also contain other nutrients in excess to what is found in blood.
evidence: This is based on comparison of media composition to blood composition.

claim: The way nutrients are used in tumors can be different from what is observed in cell culture.
source: Several studies examining tumor metabolism in mice and humans have suggested that the way nutrients are used in tumors can be different from what is observed in cell culture.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Increased glucose consumption and lactate secretion observed in most cells in culture is also observed in tumors.
source: While increased glucose consumption and lactate secretion observed in most cells in culture is also observed in tumors (Davidson et al., 2016; Hensley et al., 2016; Marin-Valencia et al., 2012; Mashimo et al., 2014; Sellers et al., 2015; Tardito et al., 2015), glutamine oxidation and anaplerosis can differ between both lung and glial tumors and cell lines derived from these tumors in culture (Davidson et al., 2016; Marin-Valencia et al., 2012; Tardito et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Glutamine oxidation and anaplerosis can differ between lung and glial tumors and cell lines derived from these tumors in culture.
source: While increased glucose consumption and lactate secretion observed in most cells in culture is also observed in tumors (Davidson et al., 2016; Hensley et al., 2016; Marin-Valencia et al., 2012; Mashimo et al., 2014; Sellers et al., 2015; Tardito et al., 2015), glutamine oxidation and anaplerosis can differ between both lung and glial tumors and cell lines derived from these tumors in culture (Davidson et al., 2016; Marin-Valencia et al., 2012; Tardito et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Culturing glioblastoma cells in serum-like medium (SMEM) results in decreased glutamine utilization and a requirement to net produce glutamine from other carbon sources.
source: Culturing glioblastoma cells in serum-like medium (SMEM) results in decreased glutamine utilization and a requirement to net produce glutamine from other carbon sources, similar to what is observed in glioblastoma in vivo (Tardito et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The bulk of TCA cycle carbon in culture systems can be accounted for from glucose and glutamine.
source: In culture systems, the bulk of TCA cycle carbon can be accounted for from glucose and glutamine.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from metabolic tracing studies.

claim: The sources of anaplerotic TCA cycle carbon in tumors are not fully understood.
source: However, the sources of anaplerotic TCA cycle carbon in tumors are not fully understood despite the increased contribution of glucose anaplerosis in some settings (Davidson et al., 2016; Hensley et al., 2016; Sellers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Addition of cystine to adult bovine serum increases A549 incorporation of glutamine carbon into the TCA cycle, but not to the same levels as in RPMI.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, addition of cystine to adult bovine serum increases A549 incorporation of glutamine carbon into the TCA cycle, but not to the same levels observed when the same cells are cultured in RPMI (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A549 cells grown in adult bovine serum are more resistant to CB-839 than A549 cells grown in RPMI with low levels of cystine.
source: Additionally, A549 cells grown in adult bovine serum are also more resistant to CB-839 than A549 cells grown in RPMI with low levels of cystine (10 µM) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Alternative anaplerotic carbon sources are available in adult bovine serum that contribute to glutaminase independence.
source: These results suggest that alternative anaplerotic carbon source(s) are available in adult bovine serum that contribute to further glutaminase independence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Environment plays a fundamental role in determining the metabolic program of cancer cells beyond oncogenic mutations.
source: Beyond the contribution of oncogenic mutations to reprogramming cellular metabolism, environment also plays a fundamental role in determining the metabolic program of cancer cells.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Environmental cystine level is one variable that can alter how nutrients are used by cancer cells.
source: We find that environmental cystine level is one variable that can alter how nutrients are used by cancer cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Selection of media conditions is essential to maximize the in vivo relevance of targets identified by metabolic gene vulnerability screens.
source: Based on our results, selection of media conditions will be essential to maximize the in vivo relevance of targets identified by screens to find metabolic gene vulnerabilities.
evidence: This is an implication and recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: A549 cells grow exponentially with a doubling time of ~48 hr when cultured in bovine serum.
source: A549 cells grow exponentially with a doubling time of ~48 hr when cultured in bovine serum (Figure 1D) and can be maintained indefinitely in such medium (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A549 cells can be maintained indefinitely in bovine serum.
source: A549 cells grow exponentially with a doubling time of ~48 hr when cultured in bovine serum (Figure 1D) and can be maintained indefinitely in such medium (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is based on the authors' experimental observations.

claim: In A549 subcutaneous xenograft tumors, there is little labeling of intratumoral glutamate, TCA cycle intermediates, and aspartate from [U-13C5]glutamine despite the presence of labeled glutamine.
source: Consistent with previous results (Davidson et al., 2016), there was little labeling of intratumoral glutamate, TCA cycle intermediates, and aspartate from [U-13C5]glutamine despite the presence of labeled glutamine in the tumors (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation.

claim: Only ~25% of glutamate is derived from glutamine in A549 tumors in vivo.
source: Normalization of tumor m + 5 glutamate label to m + 5 glutamine labeling indicates that only ~25% of glutamate is derived from glutamine in these tumors.
evidence: This is based on calculation from experimental data.

claim: When A549 cells are cultured in RPMI, 80% of glutamate is derived from glutamine.
source: In contrast, when A549 cells are cultured in RPMI-based media with [U-13C5]glutamine added to a similar enrichment of ~33%, we find that ~27% of glutamate is glutamine derived, which when normalized to glutamine enrichment indicates that 80% of glutamate is derived from glutamine under these conditions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on calculation from experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When A549 cells are cultured in RPMI, more than 60% of the carbon in aspartate and other TCA cycle intermediates is derived from glutamine.
source: Additionally, when the cells are cultured in RPMI, more than 60% of the carbon in aspartate and other TCA cycle intermediates was derived from glutamine (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Glutamine is a major TCA cycle carbon source for A549 cells in culture.
source: This is consistent with glutamine being a major TCA cycle carbon source for A549 cells in culture, and demonstrates that compared to standard culture conditions tumors derived from these cells use less glutamine in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Tumors derived from A549 cells use less glutamine in vivo compared to standard culture conditions.
source: This is consistent with glutamine being a major TCA cycle carbon source for A549 cells in culture, and demonstrates that compared to standard culture conditions tumors derived from these cells use less glutamine in vivo.
evidence: This is based on comparison of in vitro and in vivo experimental data.
